title: ASIC rip-off crackdown eyes private credit
full_text:
Sarah Court, the new boss of the Australian Securities & Investments Commission, said the regulator was keen to capitalise on taking the banking industry to task over faulty mortgage offset accounts, by scrutinising private credit lenders.
On Wednesday, ASIC revealed widespread issues across the banking sector warning many lenders were slugging homeowners with higher interest rates after failing to calculate interest properly for borrowers with an offset account.
Australia’s banks attempted to minimise the issue by saying just 1 per cent of accounts were affected by the calculation error. But Ms Court said it was unclear exactly how many customers were being duped. She would make “no comment” when asked if bankers should lose their bonuses over the rip-off.
But the ASIC chair scorched banks for failing on the most basic of tasks. She also bemoaned how so many banks didn’t know they were failing to calculate interest correctly, or sufficiently investigating when customers complained.
Ms Court is keen to know if private credit lenders are also fudging interest rates, as ASIC advances its sweep of the sector in a deliberate regulatory push. The ASIC chair dangled the prospect of enforcement action against the banking sector through the courts.
Last year, ASIC sued ANZ, settling on a fine of $125m for failing to calculate interest properly on savings accounts.
Ms Court said ASIC was “continually reviewing our enforcement book”. In a series of flying meetings with bank management, she believes the message has been conveyed.
Ms Court told The Australian ASIC had shared “a list of all the kinds of issues that ASIC is dealing with”. These included things such as the scam prevention framework, but would not expand on the rest of the issues.
Ms Court said ASIC had equally made it clear to banks the regulator was keen to act on Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ orders that burdensome rules be wound back. Earlier this month, Dr Chalmers told ASIC to strike “the right balance between supporting productivity and investment” as well as reducing the “regulatory burden on businesses”.
The banks criticised ASIC over litigation targeted at lenders which self-reported failures in handling hardship applications from customers.
ASIC sued and extracted penalties from Westpac, Commonwealth Bank, and National Australia Bank in quick succession last year.
But it is the secretive non-bank credit operatives that have grown in importance across the financial sector, lending to homebuyers as well as major commercial property developers.
As revealed in The Australian, lenders are also concerned about the conduct of borrowers, with reports made to ASIC about the adequacy of Sydney developer Bathla Group’s disclosures.
Last week, former Reserve Bank governor Phillip Lowe told The Australian he was concerned about Australia’s private credit market: “The key issues there are the quality of the loans that are being made,” he said.
“There are people in the industry who are very good at discerning what quality the underlying companies are, and there are probably some people who are not so good.
“And in the area that’s not so good, there are likely big problems.” Metrics Credit Partners boss Andrew Lockhart told The Australian on Wednesday the sector had to lift its standards, given private credit had an important role to play in the economy.
“The quality of the underwriting and the loss experience that investors are exposed to will be a key determinant as to whether managers are successful or not,” he said.
Private credit had a “social licence” which meant a good outcome for investors and workers.
But he warned of a tough 9-12 months ahead for economic activity, which could translate to more distress for lenders. “What we would say is there is a greater risk if there is any move by government to start to curb immigration numbers,” Mr Lockhart volunteered.
